newsitem.title: UK: Dollar seen rising by default as mark shivers.
newsitem.headline: Dollar seen rising by default as mark shivers.

text.p: The prospect of further mark selling will continue to energise the dollar after it got an extra filip from Federal Reserve Chairman Alan Greenspan's upbeat assessment on long-term U.S. economic prospects, analysts said.

Even though Greenspan played down the prospect of an early rise in U.S. interest rates in his Humphrey-Hawkins testimony on Tuesday, the dollar took its cue from soaring U.S. asset markets. It spurted above 1.83 marks for the first time since August 1991.
The dollar's rise dealt a further blow to the mark, and the German unit's burial on its cross rates - a key feature in the foreign exchange market this summer - continued.
"Traders are selling the mark against the world, and that's the story behind the dollar's rally," said Paul Lambert, currency economist at UBS.
"It's set to continue because the market is not short marks yet, and I won't rule out seeing the 2 mark level on the dollar," said Lambert.
On Wednesday, the German currency fell to over 4 1/2 year lows of 4.28 against the Swedish crown, to a 23-month low at 62.97 against the yen and to a 10-month low against the Swiss franc at 81.19.
Against soar-away sterling, the mark fell below 3.08 marks, its lowest since September 1989.

The mark's curse is the growing confidence among investors that membership of European economic and monetary union (EMU) will be broad-based and that the single European currency will be born as planned in 1999.
Bubbling EMU optimism has helped to boost free floating currencies unlikely to take part in the the first wave of EMU, such as the Swedish crown, the Swiss franc and sterling.

France's virtual admission this week that it will miss the Maastricht deficit criterion of 3.0 percent has added to the mark's grief. Comments from Germany and France since showed that this is unlikely to hamper EMU plans.

"All this provides the dollar with a positive backdrop and Greenspan's comments add to its upwards momentun," said Brian Martin, chief economist forex at BZW. The dollar is set to head higher into a new trading range above 1.92 marks, he added.
Greenspan said the current stance of monetary policy may have to be changed at some point, but at present, demand growth appeared to have moderated.
The combination of robust growth with low inflation was due at least partly to massive investment in technology which had improved long-term economic prospects, said Greenspan.

Analysts said Greenspan's testimony also indicated the Fed's satisfaction with the dollar's strength. The strong dollar was helping to curb inflation, and high dollar demand meant the current account gap was not a problem, said Greenspan.

"The dollar has also benefited from the expected continuation of foreign inflows into U.S. markets, particularly at a time of so much uncertainty in other parts of the world," said Tim Fox, treasury economist at Standard Chartered.

The case for stable interest rates in Germany was highlighted in a Reuters poll of 30 economists published on Wednesday. It showed the German economy will miss the government's 1997 growth goal of 2.5 percent.
Not until 1998 will the economy grow at a pace of 2.5 percent, and analysts on average expect growth for the whole of next year to reach 2.7 percent, the poll said.
Weak demand coupled with the nagging problem of high unemployment, running at over 11 percent, mean German credit is unlikely to be tightened any time soon.
That provides the dollar with an attractive interest rate premium over mark assets, analysts said.

The dollar's performance against the yen has been poor though as the Japanese unit notched up gains against the flagging mark. The yen has also attracted flows out of ailing Asian currencies into Japan, traders said.

The Asian currency crisis has been an added advantage for the dollar but analysts said the speculative nature of the onslaught on those units was unlikely to provide long-lasting support for the dollar.
